finding: An optional pair of small divisibility-lattice schematics is warranted to clarify the four order-theoretic operations and the source's left/right terminology. No diagram is present in the captures, but their rendering is clean; absence alone is not a rendering defect.

left_divisibility_geometry.order: a <=_L x iff x = a c for some positive braid c; a is a left divisor, with the cofactor appended on the right.
left_divisibility_geometry.lcm: a vee_L b is a common left multiple (a and b lie below it) and the least upper bound among common left multiples; equivalently it left-divides every common left multiple.
left_divisibility_geometry.gcd: a wedge_L b is a common left divisor (it lies below both a and b) and the greatest lower bound among common left divisors; every common left divisor lies below it.
left_divisibility_geometry.word_formula: For [u]=a and [v]=b, a vee_L b = [u Theta(u,v)] = [v Theta(v,u)]. Theta is appended on the right, although this is the join for the left-divisibility order.

right_divisibility_transport: Word reversal rho is an involutive anti-automorphism of the monoid, and it transports the left order to the right order: a <=_L b iff rho(a) <=_R rho(b). Thus it carries joins/meets for <=_L to joins/meets for <=_R without reversing the poset inequality. It reverses multiplication order; it does not turn a least upper bound into a greatest lower bound.
diagram_guidance: Use order arrows upward. For either order, place a wedge b below a and b, and a vee b above a and b; indicate the lower-bound/upper-bound extremality. A paired right-order picture can be labelled as the image under rho. Keep the suffix formula and the alternative literature phrase 'right-lcm' distinct: that phrase refers to extending words on the right, while this source calls the result vee_L because it is the join for <=_L.
source_check: The theorem defines <=_L by x = a c and <=_R by x = c a. Part (a) says the left lcm left-divides every common left multiple; part (b) says the left gcd is a common left divisor divisible on the left by every common left divisor. Part (c) transports both operations via rho. The finite-family claim excludes the empty family; for n<=1 the monoid is trivial.
